661.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
661.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak makes mastery of one's own mind the true victory, from which mastery of the world follows.
661.tie_back: The Kural says firmness in action is really firmness of mind, and all other strength is something else; Guru Nanak likewise places the decisive strength in the conquered mind.
661.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Jap (Japji Sahib, Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
661._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the mind as the seat of real strength; Guru Nanak's aim is spiritual self-mastery rather than success in practical undertakings.

662.quote_or_event: After Guru Arjan's martyrdom in 1606, the sixth Guru, Hargobind, took up his guruship girded with two swords, following his father's advice to maintain an army; he trained a force, moved his base to the Punjab hills, and later fought several battles with the Mughals.
662.explanation: Guru Hargobind both prepared against further harm and refused to let the community be broken once persecution had struck.
662.tie_back: The Kural gives two rules of firmness: guard against harm before it comes, and do not give way when it has come; Guru Hargobind's response to his father's martyrdom shows both.
662.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Development of the Sikh Community
662._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: a historical example that fits the two-part rule, but it concerns a community's survival rather than the Kural's general maxim on carrying out tasks.

663.quote_or_event: On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur, according to Sikh tradition, Guru Gobind Singh asked for five Sikhs to offer their heads and took each volunteer into his tent; only at the end did he come out with all five alive in new garments and reveal his purpose, founding the Khalsa.
663.explanation: The Guru kept his design hidden until it was complete, so the meaning of the event became clear only when he presented the five beloved ones (panj pyare).
663.tie_back: The Kural says true capability carries a task through so it becomes known only when finished; Guru Gobind Singh's founding of the Khalsa was disclosed only at its completion.
663.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Khalsa
663._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the tent episode, as Sikh tradition tells it, shows a plan revealed at completion, but its point is sacrifice and commitment, not the political secrecy the Kural advises.

664.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
664.explanation: Guru Nanak admits the gap between fine words and actual conduct as a common human failing.
664.tie_back: The Kural says anyone can say how a thing should be done, but doing it as said is hard; Guru Nanak names exactly that gap between speaking well and acting well.
664.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
664._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the gap between saying and doing, though Guru Nanak frames it as moral self-criticism rather than as a test of competence in carrying out plans.

665.quote_or_event: “Nanak proclaimed Lehna's succession - he earned it.”
665.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand record that Guru Nanak raised his devoted disciple Lehna (Guru Angad) to the Guruship because of his proven, steadfast service.
665.tie_back: The Kural says the firmness in action of the distinguished reaches the king and wins everyone's esteem; Lehna's steadfast service reached Guru Nanak himself and won him the highest seat.
665.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
665._accuracy_note: Next-best only: service earning recognition from the highest authority matches loosely, but this is spiritual succession, not a minister's renown at a royal court.

666.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
666.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that sustained effort (udam) and practice bring the fruit that is sought.
666.tie_back: The Kural promises that planners who are firm in carrying out their plans will attain what they aimed at; Guru Arjan likewise ties attainment to steady effort and practice.
666.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
666._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on effort leading to attainment; the effort Guru Arjan means is chiefly spiritual practice, and the Kural's stress on planning is absent.

667.quote_or_event: “Nanak seeks the company of the lowest of the low class, the very lowest of the low.”
667.explanation: Guru Nanak deliberately sides with those society despises, rejecting caste and outward status as measures of worth.
667.tie_back: The Kural warns against scorning anyone for small size or humble looks, since such people can be the linchpin of a great chariot; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to look down on the lowly.
667.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
667._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on not despising the humble; the Kural's point is that the small can be indispensable, while Guru Nanak's is spiritual solidarity against caste.

668.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately!”
668.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, urges acting at once rather than putting off what must be done.
668.tie_back: The Kural says that once a course is settled with a clear mind it should be carried out without wavering or delay; Kabir gives the same call against procrastination.
668.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
668._accuracy_note: Strong fit on acting without delay; Kabir's context is chiefly spiritual urgency, and the Kural's prior step of clear deliberation is not mentioned.

669.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
669.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes the true hero as one who holds the field whatever he suffers.
669.tie_back: The Kural tells us to carry on boldly with a worthy task even when great hardship comes; Kabir's hero who never leaves the field gives the same counsel of perseverance.
669.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
669._accuracy_note: Strong fit on perseverance through suffering; Kabir's image is martial and spiritual, while the Kural speaks of any worthy undertaking that brings joy in the end.

670.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
670.explanation: Guru Nanak demands total, unwavering commitment from anyone who would walk the Sikh path.
670.tie_back: The Kural says the world does not value those who lack firmness in action, whatever else they have; Guru Nanak likewise accepts no half-hearted follower and asks for resolve to the point of giving one's head.
670.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
670._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the demand for total firmness, but the setting is spiritual devotion, not the world's esteem for capable doers.
